claim: Capillary pericytes express α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) when detected using rapid filamentous-actin (F-actin) fixation methods such as snap freeze fixation with methanol at −20°C.
source: Using strategies that allow rapid filamentous-actin (F-actin) fixation (i.e. snap freeze fixation with methanol at −20°C) or prevent F-actin depolymerization (i.e. with F-actin stabilizing agents), we demonstrate that pericytes on mouse retinal capillaries, including those in intermediate and deeper plexus, express α-SMA.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing α-SMA detection in pericytes using methanol fixation, with quantitative vessel counts and statistical analysis (p=0.023).

claim: Pericytes on mouse retinal capillaries in the intermediate and deeper plexus express α-SMA.
source: we demonstrate that pericytes on mouse retinal capillaries, including those in intermediate and deeper plexus, express α-SMA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing α-SMA detection in different retinal plexus layers with statistical significance (p=0.03 for intermediate, p=0.01 for deeper plexus).

claim: Junctional pericytes (at capillary branch points) are more frequently α-SMA-positive compared to pericytes on linear capillary segments.
source: Junctional pericytes were more frequently α-SMA-positive relative to pericytes on linear capillary segments.
evidence: Based on observational data from immunolabeling experiments comparing different pericyte locations.

claim: Intravitreal administration of α-SMA-siRNA suppresses α-SMA expression preferentially in high order branch capillary pericytes.
source: Intravitreal administration of short interfering RNA (α-SMA-siRNA) suppressed α-SMA expression preferentially in high order branch capillary pericytes, confirming the existence of a smaller pool of α-SMA in distal capillary pericytes that is quickly lost by depolymerization.
evidence: Experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments showing differential effects on different capillary orders (p=0.005 for trend analysis).

claim: α-SMA in capillary pericytes rapidly depolymerizes during tissue fixation, evading detection by immunolabeling.
source: We conclude that capillary pericytes do express α-SMA, which rapidly depolymerizes during tissue fixation thus evading detection by immunolabeling.
evidence: Inference based on comparative experimental data showing increased detection with rapid fixation methods versus standard PFA fixation.

claim: Snap freeze fixation with methanol at −20°C yielded almost twice as many α-SMA-immunopositive microvessels compared to paraformaldehyde (PFA) fixation.
source: Snap freeze fixation of retinas with methanol at −20°C, yielded almost twice as many α-SMA-immunopositive microvessels compared to paraformaldehyde (PFA) fixation (Methanol: 441 ± 28 vessels, PFA: 254 ± 63 vessels, p=0.023; ANOVA)
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with statistical analysis comparing two fixation methods.

claim: The number of α-SMA-labeled microvessels significantly increased in fourth order capillaries with methanol fixation compared to PFA fixation.
source: The number of α-SMA-labeled microvessels significantly increased in fourth order capillaries (Methanol: 144 ± 19 vessels, PFA: 60 ± 28 vessels, p=0.003; ANOVA)
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with statistical significance for specific capillary order.

claim: Ethanol fixation did not improve α-SMA immunostaining compared to PFA fixation.
source: Ethanol fixation did not improve α-SMA immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B), suggesting that the effect of methanol was likely due to a faster fixation and not the result of a nonspecific response (e.g. protein denaturation).
evidence: Experimental data from ethanol fixation experiments shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The effect of methanol on α-SMA detection was likely due to faster fixation rather than nonspecific protein denaturation.
source: Ethanol fixation did not improve α-SMA immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B), suggesting that the effect of methanol was likely due to a faster fixation and not the result of a nonspecific response (e.g. protein denaturation).
evidence: Inference based on comparative experimental results between methanol and ethanol fixation.

claim: α-SMA-positive pericytes on capillaries were identified by NG2 or PDGRFβ co-immunolabeling.
source: In addition to their typical bump-on-a-log appearance detected by lectin, the α-SMA-positive pericytes on capillaries were identified by NG2 or PDGRFβ co-immunolabeling (Figure 2B–C)
evidence: Experimental data using multiple markers to identify pericytes, shown in Figure 2.

claim: α-SMA-positive pericytes on capillaries were identified by their red fluorescence in NG2-DsRed transgenic mice.
source: or by their red fluorescence in NG2-DsRed mice, a transgenic line that allows selective visualization of pericytes (Figure 2D).
evidence: Experimental data using transgenic mouse model shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Pericytes exhibit substantial F-actin in their processes surrounding capillaries.
source: we found substantial F-actin in pericyte processes surrounding capillaries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Experimental data using fluorescently-tagged phalloidin to detect F-actin.

claim: Most γ-actin immunostaining ran longitudinally, parallel to the capillary and pericyte plasma membrane, unlike the circular α-SMA outlining the pericyte somata and processes.
source: Most of the γ-actin immunostaining ran longitudinally, parallel to the capillary and pericyte plasma membrane, unlike the circular α-SMA outlining the pericyte somata and processes around the capillaries (Figure 4A–G).
evidence: Observational data from immunostaining experiments comparing γ-actin and α-SMA distribution patterns.

claim: γ-actin immunostaining was not detected in pericytes on capillaries after the 4th branch.
source: We did not detect any γ-actin immunostaining in pericytes on capillaries after the 4th branch.
evidence: Observational data from immunostaining experiments examining γ-actin distribution.

claim: F-actin fixation with methanol or phalloidin did not change γ-actin and α-SMA distribution patterns in vessels.
source: We did not observe a redistribution of the immunostaining patterns of the two actin isoforms when F-actin depolymerization was inhibited with phalloidin (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: Experimental data comparing distribution patterns under different fixation conditions.

claim: Jasplakinolide or phalloidin treatment significantly increased the number of α-SMA-labeling on capillaries of 5th and 6th order compared to PFA fixation.
source: We found that jasplakinolide or phalloidin treatment (Figures 1C, 2B, 3A–D and 5A–C) significantly increased the number of α-SMA-labeling on capillaries of 5th and 6th order compared to PFA fixation (5th order: jasplakinolide = 225 ± 28 vessels, phalloidin = 80 ± 19 vessels, PFA = 15 ± 7 vessels; 6th order: jasplakinolide = 123 ± 30 vessels, phalloidin = 23 ± 9 vessels, PFA = 0 ± 0 vessels, p=0.0001, ANOVA)
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with statistical analysis comparing F-actin stabilizing treatments.

claim: Jasplakinolide and phalloidin treatment revealed α-SMA-immunolabeling on 7th order capillaries compared to methanol or PFA fixation.
source: Besides this treatment revealed additional α-SMA-immunolabeling on 7th order capillaries (Figures 2B and 5C) compared to methanol or PFA fixation (jasplakinolide: 31 ± 12 vessels, phalloidin: 20 ± 6 vessels, methanol: 0 ± 0 vessels; PFA: 0 ± 0 vessels, p=0.002; ANOVA)
evidence: Quantitative experimental data showing detection in higher order capillaries with F-actin stabilization.

claim: The number of α-SMA-positive pericytes identified by methanol fixation or phalloidin treatment was significantly higher compared to PFA-fixed retinas.
source: α-SMA-positive pericytes identified by methanol fixation or phalloidin treatment also expressed NG2 and their number was significantly higher compared to PFA-fixed retinas (PFA: 509 ± 30 vessels, methanol: 883 ± 56 vessels, phalloidin: 890 ± 138 vessels, p=0.035, ANOVA)
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with statistical analysis comparing total pericyte counts.

claim: Phalloidin combined with methanol fixation confirmed abundant α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes of the intermediate retinal plexus.
source: Administration of phalloidin combined with methanol fixation also confirmed abundant α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes of the intermediate (PFA: 97 ± 23 pericytes, methanol: 424 ± 72 pericytes, phalloidin: 509 ± 79 pericytes, jasplakinolide: 497 ± 99 pericytes, p=0.03; ANOVA)
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with statistical analysis for intermediate plexus.

claim: Phalloidin combined with methanol fixation confirmed abundant α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes of the deeper retinal plexus.
source: and deeper (PFA: 4 ± 2.7 pericytes, methanol: 119 ± 27 pericytes, phalloidin: 260 ± 30 pericytes, jasplakinolide: 359 ± 96 pericytes, p=0.01; ANOVA) retinal plexus
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with statistical analysis for deeper plexus.

claim: Pericytes at the junction of two capillaries (junctional pericytes) were more frequently α-SMA-positive and exhibited a characteristic circular staining pattern wrapping microvessels.
source: Of interest, we found that pericytes at the junction of two capillaries (i.e. junctional pericytes) were more frequently α-SMA-positive and exhibited a characteristic circular staining pattern wrapping microvessels.
evidence: Observational data from immunostaining experiments comparing junctional versus linear pericytes.

claim: Pericytes on the linear segment of the capillary displayed a helical strand-like staining pattern and were less often α-SMA-positive.
source: In contrast, pericytes on the linear segment of the capillary, which displayed a helical strand-like staining pattern as reported by other groups (Nehls and Drenckhahn, 1991; Hartmann et al., 2015; Sims, 1986), were less often α-SMA-positive.
evidence: Observational data from immunostaining experiments with reference to previous literature.

claim: α-SMA-siRNA significantly suppressed α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes 48 hr after intravitreal administration.
source: α-SMA-siRNA significantly suppressed α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes 48 hr after intravitreal administration, while α-SMA expression in pericytes on upstream capillary branches and arterioles was less affected (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: Experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: α-SMA expression in pericytes on upstream capillary branches and arterioles was less affected by α-SMA-siRNA compared to distal capillary pericytes.
source: α-SMA-siRNA significantly suppressed α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes 48 hr after intravitreal administration, while α-SMA expression in pericytes on upstream capillary branches and arterioles was less affected (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: Experimental data showing differential effects of siRNA on different vessel types.

claim: A small pool of α-SMA in capillary pericytes is quickly lost by depolymerization, making its histological detection difficult relative to α-SMA-rich pericytes on pre-capillary arterioles and vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: These results are in agreement with the idea that a small pool of α-SMA in capillary pericytes is quickly lost by depolymerization, hence making its histological detection difficult relative to α-SMA-rich pericytes on pre-capillary arterioles and vascular smooth muscle cells.
evidence: Inference based on siRNA knockdown results showing differential stability of α-SMA pools.

claim: About 50% of NG2-positive pericytes on high order retinal capillaries (>5th) located in the intermediate and deeper retinal vascular plexus express α-SMA.
source: In this report, we demonstrate that about 50% of NG2-positive pericytes on high order retinal capillaries (i.e. >5th) located in the intermediate and deeper retinal vascular plexus express α-SMA (Figure 3D).
evidence: Quantitative experimental data from stereological analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Previous reports relied on α-SMA immunohistochemistry involving slow transcardial infusion of formaldehyde or PFA fixatives.
source: Previous reports relied on α-SMA immunohistochemistry involving the slow transcardial infusion of formaldehyde or PFA fixatives (Thavarajah et al., 2012)
evidence: Reference to published literature describing previous methodological approaches.

claim: Lack of or weak α-SMA detection in previous studies was likely due to rapid F-actin depolymerization leading to disruption of antibody-binding sites.
source: thus lack of or weak α-SMA detection was likely due to rapid F-actin depolymerization (Huber et al., 2013) leading to the disruption of the antibody-binding sites (Dudnakova et al., 2010).
evidence: Inference based on experimental results with support from cited literature on F-actin depolymerization and antibody binding.

claim: Phalloidin and jasplakinolide are F-actin stabilizing reagents with different pharmacological effects on F-actin.
source: we demonstrate that inhibition of α-SMA depolymerization in the intact eye using phalloidin or jasplakinolide, two F-actin stabilizing reagents with different pharmacological effects on F-actin
evidence: Established pharmacological knowledge about these compounds.

claim: Phalloidin or jasplakinolide binding to F-actin prevents depolymerization and fixes F-actin in the polymerized state.
source: Phalloidin or jasplakinolide binding to F-actin prevents depolymerization and fixes F-actin in the polymerized state (Auinger and Small, 2008; Cooper, 1987; Lee et al., 2010)
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature about the mechanism of action of these compounds.

claim: The ratio of α-SMA-positive pericytes was relatively lower in distal capillaries compared to upstream microvessels.
source: The ratio of α-SMA-positive pericytes was relatively lower to that found in upstream microvessels, consistent with previous reports showing less net O2 delivery from distal capillaries relative to proximal ones (Sakadžić et al., 2014).
evidence: Observational data from experiments with reference to previous literature on oxygen delivery.

claim: Knocking down α-SMA expression led to the disappearance of α-SMA immunostaining mainly in distal capillary pericytes.
source: Interestingly, knocking down α-SMA expression led to the disappearance of α-SMA immunostaining mainly in distal capillary pericytes, suggesting that the small pool of α-SMA in capillary pericytes is less stable than in vascular smooth muscle cells.
evidence: Experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments showing differential effects by vessel location.

claim: The small pool of α-SMA in capillary pericytes is less stable than in vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: knocking down α-SMA expression led to the disappearance of α-SMA immunostaining mainly in distal capillary pericytes, suggesting that the small pool of α-SMA in capillary pericytes is less stable than in vascular smooth muscle cells.
evidence: Inference based on differential siRNA knockdown effects in different cell types.

claim: A large population of pericytes, notably those at branching points of retinal microvessels, have the capacity to express α-SMA.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that a large population of pericytes, notably those at branching points of retinal microvessels, have the capacity to express α-SMA, which likely mediates their contraction.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data showing α-SMA expression patterns.

claim: α-SMA in pericytes likely mediates their contraction.
source: we conclude that a large population of pericytes, notably those at branching points of retinal microvessels, have the capacity to express α-SMA, which likely mediates their contraction.
evidence: Speculation based on the known contractile function of α-SMA and its detection in pericytes.

claim: γ-actin does not contribute to pericyte contractility in retinal capillary pericytes on distal order branches.
source: It has been suggested that γ-actin might contribute to pericyte contractility in cortical microvessels (Grant et al., 2017). However, our results do not support this hypothesis since we did not detect γ-actin-positive capillary pericytes on distal order branches after preventing F-actin depolymerization.
evidence: Experimental data showing absence of γ-actin in distal capillary pericytes, contrasting with cited literature.

claim: The increase in α-SMA-positivity after phalloidin or jasplakinolide was not caused by cross-reactivity between antibodies against γ- and α-isoforms.
source: The latter finding also indicates that the increase in α-SMA-positivity after phalloidin or jasplakinolide was not caused by cross-reactivity between the antibodies against γ- and α-isoforms or by accumulation of an excess amount of F-actin that might increase the immunostaining of all isoforms.
evidence: Inference based on differential distribution patterns of γ-actin and α-SMA after F-actin stabilization.

claim: The increase in α-SMA-positivity after phalloidin or jasplakinolide was not caused by accumulation of excess F-actin that might increase immunostaining of all isoforms.
source: The latter finding also indicates that the increase in α-SMA-positivity after phalloidin or jasplakinolide was not caused by cross-reactivity between the antibodies against γ- and α-isoforms or by accumulation of an excess amount of F-actin that might increase the immunostaining of all isoforms.
evidence: Inference based on specific detection patterns of different actin isoforms.

claim: The density of pericytes is high in the CNS and retina, where blood flow demand varies considerably between neighboring cell layers or groups.
source: Unlike peripheral tissues where the blood flow changes homogeneously, the density of pericytes is high in the CNS and retina, where the blood flow demand varies considerably between neighboring cell layers or groups (Kornfield and Newman, 2014; Armulik et al., 2011; Schallek et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by references to published literature on pericyte density and blood flow regulation.

claim: In vitro studies and recent in vivo brain studies have provided evidence that capillary pericytes contract or dilate in response to vasoactive mediators.
source: In vitro studies and recent in vivo brain studies have provided a growing body of evidence that capillary pericytes contract or dilate in response to vasoactive mediators (Peppiatt et al., 2006; Fernández-Klett et al., 2010; Puro, 2007).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited literature on pericyte contractility.

claim: Blood flow regulation with fine spatial resolution may be essential for tissues with high functional specialization such as the brain and retina.
source: This blood flow regulation with fine spatial resolution may be essential for tissues with high functional specialization such as the brain and retina.
evidence: Speculation based on the functional characteristics of brain and retina tissue.

claim: Retinal capillary dilation in response to light stimulus is layer-specific.
source: The retinal capillary dilation in response to light stimulus is reportedly layer-specific (Kornfield and Newman, 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by reference to published literature.

claim: A previous study reported robust capillary dilation in the intermediate retinal plexus but failed to detect α-SMA expression most likely due to the use of PFA-based fixation.
source: In line with our findings showing clear α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes of the intermediate plexus, the latter study reported robust capillary dilation in this region, but failed to detect α-SMA expression most likely due to the use of PFA-based fixation (Kornfield and Newman, 2014).
evidence: Inference connecting functional findings from cited literature with methodological limitations.

claim: A recent study using transgenic mice confirmed the contractile capacity of microvascular pericytes in the cortex in vivo.
source: A recent study using transgenic mice expressing fluorescent proteins driven by the NG2 or α-SMA promoters also confirmed the contractile capacity of microvascular pericytes in the cortex in vivo
evidence: Reference to published literature on pericyte contractility.

claim: Hill et al. proposed classifying NG2- and α-SMA-expressing contractile cells as smooth muscle cells rather than pericytes.
source: however, it proposed a radical redefinition by classifying the NG2- and α-SMA-expressing (contractile) cells as smooth muscle cells, rather than pericytes, as they would have conventionally been named under the original Zimmermann definition used since 1923 (Hill et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to published literature proposing alternative cell classification.

claim: The existence of at least three sub-classes of pericytes and transitional forms from smooth muscle cells has been a matter of confusion.
source: The existence of at least three sub-classes of pericytes and transitional forms from smooth muscle cells (Zimmermann, 1923) has been a matter of confusion, emphasizing the need for an unambiguous definition of pericyte sub-classes and their corresponding specialized functions.
evidence: Statement referencing historical literature and acknowledging ongoing scientific debate.

claim: Rouget first discovered pericytes in 1873 and observed that these cells might serve as contractile entities to regulate microcirculatory blood flow.
source: When Rouget first discovered pericytes in 1873, he observed that these cells might serve as contractile entities to regulate microcirculatory blood flow because of their structure and position on microvessels (Rouget, 1873).
evidence: Historical reference to the original discovery and hypothesis about pericyte function.

claim: The idea that pericytes regulate microcirculatory blood flow was challenged based on findings that microcirculatory blood flow is largely regulated by upstream arterioles rich in α-SMA.
source: However, this idea was later challenged based on findings that microcirculatory blood flow is largely regulated by upstream arterioles rich in α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), the contractile protein present in vascular smooth muscle cells.
evidence: Summary of historical scientific debate about blood flow regulation.

claim: Studies in the past three decades reported that most capillary pericytes in the central nervous system contained little or no α-SMA.
source: A number of studies in the past three decades reported that most capillary pericytes in the central nervous system contained little or no α-SMA, whereas α-SMA was detected in pericytes located on pre-capillary arterioles and post-capillary venules (Bandopadhyay et al., 2001; Nehls and Drenckhahn, 1991; Kur et al., 2012; Kornfield and Newman, 2014; Armulik et al., 2011).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: α-SMA was detected in pericytes located on pre-capillary arterioles and post-capillary venules in previous studies.
source: whereas α-SMA was detected in pericytes located on pre-capillary arterioles and post-capillary venules (Bandopadhyay et al., 2001; Nehls and Drenckhahn, 1991; Kur et al., 2012; Kornfield and Newman, 2014; Armulik et al., 2011).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: Recent in vitro and in vivo functional studies have demonstrated that a subgroup of capillary pericytes are contractile in the brain and retina.
source: In contrast, recent in vitro and in vivo functional studies have demonstrated that a subgroup of capillary pericytes are contractile in the brain and retina, and have the capacity to regulate the microcirculation by contracting and relaxing in response to physiological (i.e. neurovascular coupling) as well as pharmacological stimuli (Kornfield and Newman, 2014; Hall et al., 2014; Peppiatt et al., 2006; Fernández-Klett et al., 2010).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited functional studies.

claim: Capillary pericytes have the capacity to regulate microcirculation by contracting and relaxing in response to physiological and pharmacological stimuli.
source: recent in vitro and in vivo functional studies have demonstrated that a subgroup of capillary pericytes are contractile in the brain and retina, and have the capacity to regulate the microcirculation by contracting and relaxing in response to physiological (i.e. neurovascular coupling) as well as pharmacological stimuli (Kornfield and Newman, 2014; Hall et al., 2014; Peppiatt et al., 2006; Fernández-Klett et al., 2010).
evidence: Summary of functional findings from cited literature.

claim: Hall et al. showed that capillaries covered by pericytes dilate before arterioles in response to neuronal stimulus in situ.
source: Importantly, Hall et al. showed that capillaries covered by pericytes dilate before arte-rioles in response to neuronal stimulus in situ (Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: Specific finding from cited literature on temporal dynamics of vascular response.

claim: An increase in astrocytic calcium was shown to mediate brain capillary changes in response to metabolic demand.
source: Recently, an increase in astrocytic calcium was shown to mediate brain capillary changes in response to metabolic demand (Mishra et al., 2016).
evidence: Specific finding from cited literature on astrocyte-mediated capillary regulation.

claim: Biesecker et al. showed that calcium signaling in Müller cell endfeet was sufficient to evoke capillary dilation in the retina.
source: Similarly, Biesecker et al. showed that calcium signaling in Müller cell endfeet was sufficient to evoke capillary dilation in the retina (Biesecker et al., 2016).
evidence: Specific finding from cited literature on Müller cell-mediated capillary regulation.

claim: Kisler et al. reported that transgenic mice with a decreased number of pericytes had deficient neurovascular coupling and reduced oxygen delivery to the brain.
source: Kisler et al. reported that transgenic mice with a decreased number of pericytes had deficient neurovascular coupling and reduced oxygen delivery to the brain (Kisler et al., 2017), providing additional evidence for the importance of pericytes in blood flow regulation.
evidence: Specific finding from cited literature on pericyte function in neurovascular coupling.

claim: Functional and histological studies provide evidence for the presence of a bona fide contractile machinery in capillary pericytes.
source: Collectively, these experiments strongly suggest the presence of a bona fide contractile machinery in capillary pericytes.
evidence: Inference based on synthesis of multiple cited functional studies.

claim: Hill et al. dismissed the idea of pericytes being contractile by redefining α-SMA-expressing pericytes as smooth muscle cells.
source: However, a recent paper dismisses the idea of pericytes being contractile by redefining α-SMA-expressing pericytes as smooth muscle cells (Hill et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to published literature presenting an alternative interpretation.

claim: Small amounts of α-SMA in capillary pericytes may be rapidly depolymerized during transcardial perfusion and fixation.
source: To address this paradox between functional and histological findings, we hypothesized that small amounts of α-SMA in capillary pericytes may be rapidly depolymerized during transcardial perfusion and fixation thus evading detection by immunolabeling.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed to explain discrepancy between functional and histological findings.

claim: α-SMA in pericytes has been detected by electron microscopy in which small amounts of α-SMA can be identified.
source: Consistent with this idea, α-SMA in pericytes has been detected by electron microscopy in which small amounts of α-SMA can be identified (Toribatake et al., 1997; Le Beux and Willemot, 1978; Ho, 1985; Nakano et al., 2000)
evidence: Reference to published electron microscopy studies detecting α-SMA in pericytes.

claim: α-SMA in pericytes has been detected by in vitro studies in which fixation is more rapidly achieved.
source: or by in vitro studies in which fixation is more rapidly achieved (Herman and D'Amore, 1985).
evidence: Reference to published in vitro studies detecting α-SMA in pericytes.

claim: When F-actin depolymerization was prevented by F-actin stabilizing agents or by snap fixation, α-SMA was detected in a much larger fraction of microvascular pericytes.
source: Here, we show that when filamentous-actin (F-actin) depolymerization was prevented by F-actin stabilizing agents or by snap fixation, we detected α-SMA in a much larger fraction of microvascular pericytes, including capillary pericytes placed on the intermediate and deeper retinal vascular beds.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the current study.

claim: The inhibition trend of α-SMA by siRNA being more prominent on high order branches was statistically significant (p=0.005).
source: The inhibition trend being more prominent on high order branches was statistically significant (p=0.005) with non-parametric Jonckheere-terpstra test for trend analysis.
evidence: Statistical analysis of siRNA knockdown data showing trend across capillary orders.

claim: Western blotting showed that α-SMA protein levels were reduced in α-SMA-siRNA injected retinas but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
source: Western blotting (D–E) (scrambled-siRNA, n = 3, 1.22 ± 0.32 a.u.; α-SMA-siRNA, n = 3, 0.93 ± 0.23 a.u., p=0.4; Student's t-test)
evidence: Quantitative Western blot data with statistical analysis.

claim: qRT-PCR showed that α-SMA-mRNA levels were reduced in α-SMA-siRNA injected retinas but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
source: qRT-PCR (F) (scrambled-siRNA, n = 3, 1.51 ± 0.33 a.u.; α-SMA-siRNA, n = 3, 1.14 ± 0.32 a.u., p=0.7; Student's t-test)
evidence: Quantitative qRT-PCR data with statistical analysis.

claim: Large amounts of α-SMA in proximal microvessels possibly masked the inhibition in high order branches with small pools of α-SMA in Western blot and qRT-PCR analyses.
source: show that both α-SMA protein and α-SMA-mRNA levels were reduced in α-SMA-siRNA injected retinas but the difference did not reach statistical significance possibly because the large amounts of α-SMA in proximal microvessels masked the inhibition in high order branches with small pools of α-SMA.
evidence: Inference explaining why statistical significance was not reached in whole-retina analyses.

claim: Detection of minute pools of α-SMA in small soma and processes of pericytes might be difficult to visualize in transgenic mice due to dispersion of limited membrane-bound reporter protein over large surface area.
source: It is possible that the detection of the minute pool of α-SMA in small soma and processes of pericytes does not only depend on the fixation method, but might also be difficult to visualize in transgenic mice due to dispersion of the limited amount of membrane-bound reporter protein over the relatively large surface area of the pericyte membrane.
evidence: Speculation about technical limitations in transgenic reporter systems.

claim: Incomplete (mosaic-like) fluorescent protein expression after tamoxifen injection in inducible transgenic mice can account for failure to visualize low levels of α-SMA labeling at capillary pericytes.
source: Moreover, incomplete (mosaic-like) fluorescent protein expression after tamoxifen injection in inducible transgenic mice, in which Cre recombinase expression is driven by the α-SMA promoter, can also account for the failure to visualize low levels of α-SMA labeling at capillary pericytes (Hill et al., 2015; Hartmann et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference about technical limitations in inducible transgenic systems with reference to literature.

claim: Phalloidin and jasplakinolide were especially effective in revealing α-SMA expression in 7th order capillaries.
source: Phalloidin and jasplakinolide were especially effective in revealing α-SMA expression in 7th order capillaries, suggesting that their small α-SMA pool rapidly depolymerizes during tissue processing (p=0.002, ANOVA followed by Dunnett's test).
evidence: Quantitative experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The small α-SMA pool in 7th order capillaries rapidly depolymerizes during tissue processing.
source: Phalloidin and jasplakinolide were especially effective in revealing α-SMA expression in 7th order capillaries, suggesting that their small α-SMA pool rapidly depolymerizes during tissue processing
evidence: Inference based on differential effectiveness of F-actin stabilizers in distal capillaries.

claim: Seventy-three Swiss albino mice and eleven NG2-DsRed mice were used in the study.
source: Seventy three Swiss albino (21–35 g), eleven NG2-DsRed (Schallek et al., 2013) mice were housed under diurnal lighting conditions (12 hr darkness and 12 hr light) and fed ad libitum.
evidence: Methodological description of animal subjects used in experiments.

claim: Animal experiments were approved by the Hacettepe University Animal Experiments Local Ethics Committee (2012/63).
source: Animal housing, care, and application of experimental procedures were all carried out in accordance with the institutional guidelines and approved by the Hacettepe University Animal Experiments Local Ethics Committee (2012/63)
evidence: Statement of ethical approval for animal experiments.

claim: Animal experiments were approved by committee guidelines on animal resources at the University of Rochester.
source: committee guidelines on animal resources at the University of Rochester (Rochester, New York)
evidence: Statement of ethical approval for animal experiments.

claim: Animal experiments were approved by the Canadian Council on Animal Care and CRCHUM.
source: and the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care and the Centre de Recherche du Centre Hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CRCHUM, Montreal, Quebec, Canada).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval for animal experiments.
